title: It Could Always Be Worse
text:
A Yiddish folk tale tells of a poor man who lived in a one-room hut with his wife, his mother and his many children. The house was so crowded and noisy that he could not bear it. The children fought, his wife and mother quarreled, and there was no peace anywhere. At his wits' end, he went to the rabbi for advice.

The rabbi asked whether he had any animals. A few chickens, the man said, a rooster, a goose, a goat and a cow. "Take the chickens, the rooster and the goose into the house with you," said the rabbi. The man was puzzled but did as he was told. Now the hut was worse than ever, full of clucking and crowing and honking.

He went back to the rabbi, who told him to bring in the goat. When he came back again, the rabbi told him to bring in the cow as well. Each time the poor man came back more desperate. The house was chaos: animals underfoot, feathers in the soup, nowhere to sleep.

At last the rabbi said: "Go home and let all the animals out of the house." The man did. That night his family slept peacefully. The hut seemed quiet and spacious. He went back to the rabbi and thanked him: life had never been so sweet.
lesson: A crowded, noisy home can feel unbearable until we remember how much worse it could be. Gratitude often depends on what we compare our life with.
people: A poor man, his family, a rabbi
source: Yiddish folk tradition; retold by Margot Zemach, It Could Always Be Worse (1976)
